title.official: Permission of Court to amendment before or after close of pleadings

division.heading: Request for Particulars, Amendments to Pleadings and Close of Pleadings

operative_text.controlling:
3.65(1)  Subject to subrule (5), before or after close of pleadings,
the Court may give permission to amend a pleading.
(2)  If the Court gives permission for a pleading to be amended, the
Court must specify the time period within which the amended
pleading must be filed and served.
(3)  An order giving permission to amend a pleading under this rule
ceases to have effect unless the amended pleading is filed and
served within the time specified by the Court.
(4)  If the Court directs or allows a pleading to be amended at trial,
(a) the amendment must be recorded in writing by the court
clerk, and
(b) no order need be filed.
(5)  This rule does not apply to an amendment to a pleading to add,
remove, substitute or correct the name of a party to which rule 3.74
applies.

commentary.text: Rule 3.65 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.65. 1. Overview In Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v. Crossroads C & I Distributors, 2011 ABQB 51, 2011 CarswellAlta 108, Justice Poelman said, at paragraphs 42–46: 42 Rule 3.65 gives no substantive guidelines on when amendments not adding parties should be granted. Apart from formal requirements, it simply states that “the Court may give permission to amend a pleading.” 43 The most analogous former provision is rule 132, which stated as follows: The court may at any stage of the proceedings allow any party to alter or amend his pleadings or other proceedings in such manner and on such terms as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real question in issue between the parties. 44 The reference to “purpose of determining the real question in issue between the parties” does not appear in rule 3.65. However, rule 1.2(2)(a) includes that purpose in the overall purpose and intention of the new Alberta Rules of Court. Thus, rule 3.65 cannot be seen as a change from the approach taken by the courts under the former rule 132. 45 The principles to be applied on amendment applications, established by the authorities under the formal rules, were recently summarized by Wittmann C.J.Q.B. [in Dow Chemical Canada Inc. v. Nova Chemicals Corporation 2010 ABQB 524, at paragraphs 20-21] as follows: [20] Generally, any pleading can be amended no matter how careless or late is the party seeking to amend: Balm v. 3512061 Canada Ltd., 2003 ABCA 98, 327 A.R. 149 at para. 43. This is referred to in Balm as the “classic rule”. [21] The classic rule is subject to four major exceptions: Canadian Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Canadian Commercial Bank, 2000 ABQB 440, 269 A.R. 49 at para. 11; Foda v. Capital Health Region, 2007 ABCA 207 at para. 10; see also C.H.S. v. Alberta (Director of Child Welfare), 2006 ABQB 528, 403 A.R. 103 at para. 11, aff'd 2006 ABCA 355, 401 A.R. 215. Those exceptions are as follows: 1. the amendment would cause serious prejudice to the opposing party, not compensable in costs; 2. the amendment requested is “hopeless” (an amendment that, if were in the original pleadings, would have been struck); 3. unless permitted by statute, the amendment seeks to add a new party or a new cause of action after the expiry of a limitation period; and 4. there is an element of bad faith associated with the failure to plead the amendment in the first instance. Therefore, if no exception applies, the pleadings can generally be amended. 46 The principles summarized by Wittmann C.J.Q.B. were not premised on particular words in the old rules. Rather, they arose from the function of pleadings before our contemporary common law courts. As stated by Bensler J. [in Newel Post Developments Ltd. v. 1402801 Alberta Ltd., 2010 ABQB 660 at paragraph 18]: [18] This discretion [to amend pleadings] exists because “pleadings are not a meaningless ritual incantation or medieval superstition; they fulfil the first rule of natural justice, knowledge of the case against one”: Waquan v. Canada, 2002 ABCA 110, 303 A.R. 43, 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 1 at para. 85. Furthermore, with the Court bound to decide a matter upon the issues pled before it, accurate pleadings are necessary for just decisions. In Quadrangle Holdings Ltd. v. Coady, 2012 ABQB 22, 2012 CarswellAlta 86, 531 A.R. 48, Justice McCarthy relied on Manson Insulation Products Ltd., and said, at paragraph 22: Therefore, it appears that under the new rules pleadings can be amended no matter how careless or late is the party seeking to amend. In Elbow River Marketing Ltd. Partnership v. Canada Clean Fuels Inc., 2012 ABQB 277, 2012 CarswellAlta 790, 538 A.R. 145, 62 Alta. L.R. (5th) 359; reversed 2012 ABCA 328, 2012 CarswellAlta 1914, 539 A.R. 68, 69 Alta. L.R. (5th) 22, at paragraphs 19-20, Justice Tilleman followed the law set out above from Ignition Energy Ltd. v. Direct Energy Marketing Ltd., 2011 ABQB 90, 2011 CarswellAlta 195, and Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v. Crossroads C & I Distributors, 2011 ABQB 51, 2011 CarswellAlta 108. In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2012 ABQB 679, 2012 CarswellAlta 2257, 549 A.R. 72, 79 Atla. L.R. (5th) 1; [affirmed 2013 ABCA 87] Madam Justice Hughes also quoted with approval Whittmann C.J.Q.B. in Dow Chemical Canada Inc. v. Nova Chemicals Corp., 2010 ABQB 524 at paragraph 36. Her Ladyship then discussed amendment applications which do not require evidence. At paragraphs 47-48, her Ladyship said: 47 Amendments which are trivial, such as those that do not seek to impose any liability on new defendants, or those that are purely ancillary, do not require evidence: Balm at paras 9 and 23. See also Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada, 2002 ABCA 110 at para 26, 303 AR 43 [“Mikisew”] 48 Amendments pleading a new cause of action or claim arising from facts already plead in existing pleadings filed in time, also require little if any evidence. In Balm, Côté JA observed at para 11: Paragraph 37 in the amended statement of claim is new, and is clearly a new cause of action. However, though the legal conclusion pleaded is new, the acts alleged in it are not new. It is trite law that a statement of claim need not name causes of action or draw legal conclusions. It need only plead facts. So the plaintiff could merely have sent the original defendants' counsel a letter warning that he would argue at trial that proof of such and such facts already alleged in the statement of claim would constitute the cause of action of mutuality of obligations under law merchant. See 30 Hals. Laws 7 (3rd Ed. 1959). At paragraphs 49–51, 53–56, she discussed the evidence necessary for a significant amendment: 49 The leading Alberta case respecting the evidentiary burden and the nature of the evidence required for substantive amendments to pleadings is Balm. Côté JA summarized the law at paras 25 and 26 as follows: When evidence is needed to support a significant amendment to a pleading, before the limitation period has expired, what evidence is needed? The Waquan (Mikisew) case, supra, does not address the point (except for some discussion about use of discovery evidence). I have not found much direct authority on the topic. (One reason is that England, British Columbia, and the Federal Court of Canada require no evidence at all.) One case says that the test is whether in the evidence filed to support the proposed amendment “facts were alleged from which it could be inferred that” the facts to be pleaded occurred: Wil-Ton Constr. v. Amerada Minerals Corp. (1989), 98 A.R. 296, 304 (para. 43), 69 Alta. L.R. (2d) 285 (C.A.). Chief Justice Moore held that the evidence need not be enough to prove the new allegations on a balance of probabilities: Anderson Expl. v. Pan-Alberta Gas (1998) 224 A.R. 109, 112 (para. 14). Possibly Kent J. was stating a standard when she called for “more than a scintilla of evidence”, in Firemaster Oilfield Services v. Safety Boss (Can.) (1993) (June 14 ‘96) J.D.E. 9303-20358, unrep. She said that “everyone is in agreement that the threshold is low”: ibid. The chambers judge here adverted to that standard of proof (in his paras. 15, 16). Hearsay clearly suffices: Marathon Constr. (Alta.) v. Bank of N.S. (1985) 47 Sask. R. 241 (C.A.). The appellants’ factum does not cite any authority which contradicts those propositions. Of course any admissible evidence will do. It need not be an affidavit by the party seeking to amend: Sheckter v. W. Motor Hotels (Edm.), (1985) 61 A.R. 154, 158 (M.) (para. 19). 50 It is clear from the above passage in Balm that the evidentiary standard is very low and that the type of admissible evidence to support new amendments includes hearsay evidence. 51 In CHS v. Alberta (Director of Child Welfare) 2006 ABQB 528 at para 11, 403 AR 103, aff'd 2006 ABCA 355, 401 A.R. 215, the Court considered the evidence required: Only a modest amount of evidence is needed to support an amendment. An amendment will only be refused based on an argument that it is “bound to fail on the merits” if it is clear that there is no genuine issue for trial, and the amended claim would not survive a summary judgment application. These principles are set out in a number of cases, including Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada, 2000 ABQB 899, 86 Alta. L.R. (3d) 139, 278 A.R. 375 at para. 7; Rago Millwork & Supplies Co. Ltd. v. D. Woodhouse Construction Ltd. (1981), 28 A.R. 499; W.R. v. Alberta (Attorney General), 2004 ABQB 979 at para.11; Balm v. 3512061 Canada Ltd., 2003 ABCA 98, 14 Alta. L.R. (4th) 221, 327 A.R.149 at para. 25; Brar v. Roy, 2005 ABCA 269, 371 A.R. 290 at paras. 17-18. … 53 Although only modest evidence need be provided, it must have some foundation in fact. 54 Those opposing the Defendants' proposed amendments assert that amendments must be supported by evidence of sufficient cogency, relying on JAV International Ventures Ltd v. Halliburton Group Canada Inc, 2008 ABCA 99. In that case, the respondents sought to admit affidavit evidence in support of their pleading amendments which detailed conversations that had taken place during privileged settlement negotiations. The issue before the Court was whether the evidentiary foundation supported the Respondents's position that privilege had been waived. The only comment respecting the evidentiary burden in an amendment to pleadings application is in the first sentence in para 5 which states: In the context of an application to amend the pleadings, the evidentiary burden is “modest”. At this stage of the proceedings, for purposes of the Respondents' motion to amend the pleadings, the threshold for admissibility is, in our view, prima facie evidence of sufficient cogency that the allegations have some foundation in fact. [emphasis added] 55 I find the phrase “evidence of specific cogency” in the JAV case applies to the evidentiary foundation to support the Respondent's position the privilege had been waived, and not to the evidentiary burden on an application to amend. 56 The parties opposing the Defendants' proposed amendments introduced evidence that could be found to be contrary to the evidence proffered by the Defendants. It must be remembered that the purpose of these applications is not to make findings of fact or to finally decide the issues raised in the pleadings. The evidence submitted in support of the amendments may be contradictory to other evidence submitted. I need only determine if there is “some” evidence supporting the proposed amendments. As Côté JA stated in Balm at para 13: It is for that reason that the court will authorize a party to amend his pleadings, even if he has given some examination for discovery answers inconsistent with that proposed amendment: Neogleous v. Toffolon (No. 2) (1977) 17 O.R. (2d) 453 (H.C.) at p. 455. The appellants made just that objection here. They do argue that the claim against 070 and Jonathon is hopeless, but try to do so on the basis of evidence as to lack of damage, especially a cross-examination admission by the plaintiff. This is not a motion for summary judgment by the plaintiff. Doubt avails the appellants nothing. [emphasis in original] In Attila Dogan Construction v. AMEC Americas Ltd., 2013 ABQB 525, 2013 CarswellAlta 1979, 565 A.R. 1; affirmed 2014 ABCA 74, 2014 CarswellAlta 269, 569 A.R. 308, Chief Justice Wittmann agreed with Hughes J., and said, at paragraph 21: 21 I agree with the proposition set out by Hughes J. in Canadian Natural at para. 53, that, in general, although only modest evidence need be provided, any amendment to add new facts of substance should have some basis in evidence, though the standard may be low. I further take the view that if the proposed amendment is made to add allegations of undue influence and duress, it should be supported by particulars and a somewhat higher evidentiary standard will apply. The parties directed me to no authorities that would directly support the proposition that the Court should disregard the evidence that has been brought before it on an amendment application when attempting to determine whether a proposed amendment is hopeless. It is appropriate, therefore, to briefly consider the evidence that AD has brought in support of this application in considering whether the duress and undue influence claims may proceed. In RK v. GSG, 2024 ABKB 661, additional reasons 2024 ABKB 771, Justice Mah gave the following summary of the law relating to the amendment of pleadings: [7] In considering the proposed amendments to the Statement of Claim, I have regard to the following principles established by caselaw: • While the Rules of Court authorize the Court to allow amendments, there is no provision to guide that discretion. The guidance is provided by the decided cases: AARC Society v Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, 2019 ABCA 125 at para 51. • The common law states that discretion should be exercised generously: Andritz Ltd v Quality Fabricating and Supply Ltd., 2010 ABQB 101 at para 43. Indeed, the so-called “classic rule” is that “any pleading can be amended no matter how careless or late is the party seeking to amend”: Balm v 3512061 Canada Ltd, 2003 ABCA 98 at para 43. • The rationale for this liberal approach is simple: “pleadings are not a meaningless ritual incantation or medieval superstition…they fulfil the first rule of natural justice, [which is] knowledge of the case against one”: Waquan v Canada, 2002 ABCA 110 at para 85. Insofar as amendments can help identify key issues of contention and keep matters moving expeditiously through the system, there is a strong presumption in favour of allowing amendments: AARC Society, paras 55-56. • Before granting an amendment application, the Court should consider two separate but equally-weighted interests: the litigation interests of the opposing party, and the public interest in having the matter conclude in a timely manner with as little expenditure of public and private resources as possible: AARC Society, paras 58-62. • If the amendment is merely to add particulars—rather than, for example, a new Defendant or a new cause of action—permission should be readily granted, because the prejudice to the opposing party can be presumed to be limited: Rabbit Hill Recreations Inc v Stelter, 2009 ABQB 329 at para 82. • On the whole, amendments are generally permitted, subject to narrow enumerated objections: Farm Credit Canada v Chan, 2021 ABCA 168 at para 21. If an opposing party objects to the proposed amendments, that party bears the onus of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the amendment falls within one of the exceptions: Foda v Capital Health Region, 2007 ABCA 207 at para 10; AARC Society at para 53. An amendment can be denied if: ◦ The amendment would cause serious prejudice to the opposing party that could not be compensated through enhanced costs - i.e. prejudice arising from the passage of time; ◦ The amendment is “hopeless” – i.e. that it would have been struck out if it had been in the original application; ◦ The amendment seeks to add a new party or a new cause of action after the expiration of the limitations period (unless expressly permitted by statute); or ◦ There is an element of bad faith associated with the failure to include the new information in the original pleading. [8] Caselaw further illuminates the contours of the above exceptions: • Serious prejudice ◦ Delay is closely connected to prejudice—so any prejudice arising from delay will be assessed on a case-by-case and fact-driven basis. Delay, in and of itself, does not create prejudice enough to block an application to amend. Unless there is an expired limitations period, an amendment cannot be barred simply because it is late. However, the timing of the application relative to the life-cycle of the litigation as a whole is of some relevance: Pace v Economical Mutual Insurance, 2021 ABCA 1 at paras 51-52. ◦ The party asserting prejudice bears the onus of establishing it: Balm at para 43. The passage of several years between the time when counsel should have been aware of the issue giving rise to the amendment and the actual application creates the automatic presumption of serious prejudice: Eon Energy Ltd v Ferrybank Resources Ltd, 2018 ABCA 243 at paras 26-27; Domenic Construction Ltd v Primewest Capital Corporation, 2019 ABQB 58 at para 69. • “Hopeless” ◦ An amendment application should not be granted where the claim is hopeless, such that the pleading would have been struck if originally pled: McCargar v Metis Nation of Alberta Association, 2017 ABQB 692 at para 7, aff'd 2018 ABCA 144. A pleading is hopeless only if it is clear and obvious that it contains no triable issue, which is something giving rise to a claim recognized in law: McCargar (QB) at para 19. ◦ The evidentiary threshold to support an amendment application is usually low—but after the close of pleadings, “some” evidence is required to amend: Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co Inc v AMEC America's Ltd, 2014 ABCA 74 at para 27. Where the proposed amendment raises allegations of fraud, high-handedness, or malicious conduct, there must be “good ground” or “exceptional circumstances” to permit such amendments. “Significant evidence” is required to prove “good ground”: Canadian Natural Resources Limited v Arcelormitall Tubular Products Roman SA, 2013 ABCA 87 at paras 11-12], quoting Mikisew Cree First Nation v Canada, 2002 ABCA 110. However, the applicant does not need to adduce enough evidence to show that the amended pleading can be proven at trial, or to meet the test for summary judgement: Attila Dogan at para 26. • Limitations-Barred ◦ An amendment takes retroactive effect going back to the date of the original pleading, as if it had been part of the original pleading all along: PTL Bobcat and Landscape Services Lt. v 1149218 Alberta Ltd, 2013 ABQB 158 at para 32. Any amendment that would add a new cause of action or a new party outside of the limitations period is barred, apart from statutory exception. ◦ If a cause of action has already been pled within the limitations period, then further particulars about that cause of action can be pled outside the limitations period. Under these circumstances, there is no resulting prejudice to the other party, who has had knowledge of the claim against them (in broad terms, at least) since the beginning. However, if the “particulars” go beyond the scope of the original Statement of Claim, there may be a valid limitations defense. Trying to slip in an improper amendment under the guise of “particulars” is inappropriate: Geophysical Service Incorporated v Plains Midstream Canada ULC, 2021 ABCA 55 at para 5. ◦ When amendments are sought after possible expiry of a limitation period, it is best practice to resolve the limitations issue at the time the amendment application is made. If the complexity of the facts, or the state of the record, preclude a final decision on the limitations issue, the amendments should be allowed and the Defendants be permitted to plead the limitations defense at trial: Domenic Construction Ltd v Primewest Capital Corp., 2020 ABCA 265 at paras 23-28. • Bad Faith ◦ An amendment can be barred where either the amendment itself, or its timing, shows bad faith: Hur v 726913 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 208 at paras 83-84. Bad faith involves an intention to harm the other party, to conceal information relevant to the issues, or to deceive either the other party or the Court. This requisite intent to harm, deceive, or conceal must form a significant part of the party's overall motivation: CS v MS, 2007 CanLII 20279 (ONSC) at para 17. The timing of an amendment application cannot, on its own, prove that an amendment is being brought in bad faith: 926 Capital Corp v Petro River Oil Corp, 2016 ABQB 194 at paras 33-37. The bad faith exception is not intended to punish negligent or careless delay that can be recompensed through costs: Club Industrial Trailers v Paramount Structures, 2022 ABQB 34 at paras 35-36. • Since “relevance is the foundation of pleadings”, relevance (or lack of it) is a ground upon which to deny an amendment: Angus Partnership Inc v Salvation Army (Governing Council), 2014 ABCA 423 at para 8. Further, amendments to pleadings should clarify and not obfuscate the issues before the Court. Pleadings, and amendments to pleadings, are to be as brief as possible and are meant to assist in the clarification of the issues before the Court: Devon Canada Corporation v Transcanada Power Services Ltd, 2007 ABQB 479 at para 105. An allowable amendment must be necessary for determining the real question in issue between the parties, the amendment must be useful in determining the real issues, the amendment must plead material facts, not evidence or argument and any new facts plead must be supported by evidence: Devon Canada at para 106. [9] Thus, it seems to me from the foregoing review of caselaw that an amendment must also be relevant and necessary (as described above) to be allowable. Expressed otherwise, that an amendment is “irrelevant or useless” (in terms of assisting with the issues before the Court) is a notional fifth category of exception to the general rule of permitting amendments. See also: Justice Feth's summary of the law in Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Alberta, 2024 ABKB 578 at paragraphs 16-18. At paragraphs 21-22 of that decision, Justice Feth added: [21] Where a cross-application to amend pleadings is brought in response to an application to strike, the general practice is to first determine whether the amendments are granted: United Petroleum Distributors (Calgary) v 548311 Alberta Ltd, 1998 ABCA 121 at para 5, 216 AR 116. However, the general practice may be varied if the proposed amendments will not change the result: Carbone v McMahon, 2015 ABCA 263 at para 8; Carbone v Burnett, 2019 ABQB 98 at para 38. [22] The general practice serves to clarify the pleadings before analyzing whether the Statement of Claim establishes a reasonable cause of action, rather than anticipating what the amendments might be. Either approach can be utilized. Here, the clarifying amendments are specifically delineated and relevant to the ultimate analysis, so I have chosen to rule first on the amendment application. This approach also avoids the chicken and the egg conundrum created by the Alberta Crown's position: the pleadings cannot be amended until a reasonable cause of action is found, but the search for the cause of action requires the amended pleadings to be reviewed. 2. Threshold for Amendment is Low In Ignition Energy Ltd. v. Direct Energy Marketing Ltd., 2011 ABQB 90, 2011 CarswellAlta 195, Justice Macleod said (at paragraphs 9–11): 9 Under Rule 3.65 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, the Court has broad discretion to amend pleadings: Subject to subrule (5), before or after close of pleadings, the Court may give permission to amend a pleading. This broad discretion is subject to the Court's duty not to cure non-compliance when to do so would result irreparable harm to a party under Rule 1.5(4). … 10 The Court's discretion to amend pleadings recognizes the importance of accurate pleadings. Pleadings inform the other side as to the case being put forth against them and the Court is bound to make a decision based on what is plead before it: see Waquan v. Canada, 2002 ABCA 110, 303 A.R. 43 at para. 85; see also Newel Post Developments Ltd. v. 1402801 Alberta Ltd., 2010 ABQB 660. 11 As such, the threshold required to allow an amendment is very low. As stated in Balm v. 3512061 Canada Ltd., 2003 ABCA 98, 327 A.R. 149 at para. 43, an “amendment should be allowed, no matter how careless or late, unless there is prejudice to the other side”. Absent prejudice, only a “clearly and obviously invalid” amendment should be rejected: Oregon Jack Creek Indian Band v. Canadian National Railway Co. (Motion), [1990] 1 S.C.R. 117 at p. 118. Even a doubtful plea should be allowed, so long as it is at least arguable: Balm at para. 12. 3. Amending to Allege Fraud In Condominium Corp. No. 0321365 v. 970365 Alberta Ltd., 2011 ABQB 325, 2011 CarswellAlta 2247, 518 A.R. 1, the Plaintiff brought an application to amend the Statement of Claim so that it contained an allegation that a particular asset transfer had been made “with the mutual intention or having the effect of defeating, hindering, prejudicing or delaying the Plaintiffs' claims …” and that it therefore “constitute[d] a fraudulent preference or conveyance within the meaning of the Fraudulent Preferences Act… and the Statute of Elizabeth….” No further particulars were sought to be pleaded. The Defendants opposed the application to amend on the grounds that the proposed amendment did not “have the necessary evidentiary underpinnings.” The Plaintiff “urge[d] the Court to make a distinction between the evidentiary requirements when a Plaintiff seeks to amend the claim to allege fraud and when a Plaintiff seeks to amend to allege a fraudulent intention or a fraudulent transaction. The Plaintiff [said] that, to amend to plead the latter, much less is required in the way of evidence to support the amendment.” Justice Hall said, at paragraph 4, “there is no merit to such a distinction.” His Lordship went on to say (paragraph 4): … In short “fraudulent” necessarily imports the concept of fraud. Fraudulent intention is the intention to commit fraud. A fraudulent transaction is a transaction effected by fraud. I find, therefore that the requirement of providing evidentiary underpinnings to amend a claim to allege a fraudulent intention or a fraudulent transaction is the same as the requirement when seeking to amend a claim to allege fraud. Hall, J. then discussed the type of evidence which is necessary to support an application to amend a pleading by adding an allegation of fraud. He said at paragraphs 6–9: 6 A plaintiff may allege fraud against a defendant or defendants at first instance without providing evidence of fraud, so long as the Plaintiff pleads the allegation with sufficient particularity: Rules 13.6(3) and 13.7(b) 7 However, if a plaintiff wishes to amend the claim to allege fraud against a defendant or defendants, Courts are reluctant to allow the amendment. In Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada, [2002] A.J. No. 596, 2002 CarswellAlta 603 the Alberta Court of Appeal stated, at para. 61: There must be good ground in a particular case to relax the general rule against amending to allege fraud (cite omitted). Some cases say that “exceptional circumstances” are needed. And it is impossible to show “good ground” without significant evidence, let alone particulars. 8 Mikisew was considered by Mr. Justice Gill in Evanoff Enterprises Ltd. v. Pioneer Hi-Bred Ltd., [2009] A.J. No. 400, 2009 CarswellAlta 571 at para. 49, where he says: There is a general rule against amending to allege fraud, and significant evidence is required to show that “exceptional circumstances” or “good grounds” exist: Mikisew at para. 61. Although ordinarily only a modest amount of evidence is required for amendments, a higher standard of evidence may be required for amendments to include allegations of fraud, and evidence of intent is required: ibid., see also Milne v. Columbia Health Centre Inc., 2005 ABQB 594, 383 A.R. 252 (Alta. Q.B.), at paras. 11–13. 9 In summary, significant evidence of fraud, and evidence of intent is required, in order to allow the amendment. In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2012 ABQB 679, 2012 CarswellAlta 2257, 549 A.R. 72, 79 Alta. L.R. (5th) 1; [affirmed 2013 ABCA 87] Madam Justice Hughes discussed pleadings which allege fraud. She said at paragraphs 76–78: 76 A pleading must “include a statement of any matter on which a party intends to rely that may take another party by surprise”, including breach of trust, fraud, malice or ill will, and misrepresentation: Rule 13.6(3). A pleading must also give the particulars of the alleged breach of trust, fraud, misrepresentation, or wilful default: Rule 13.7. 77 In Mikisew at para 61, the Court set out the following evidentiary foundation required for amendments alleging fraud: This proposed amendment makes a very strong sweeping allegation of fraud in 1986. The plaintiffs tendered no evidence whatever to support this amendment. Courts are reluctant to allow an amendment to raise a new plea of fraud. There must be good ground in a particular case to relax the general rule against amending to allege fraud: 2 Holmested & Gale, Ontario Judicature Act, R. 132 s. 10 (1997 rev.). Some cases say that “exceptional circumstances” are needed. And it is impossible to show “good ground” without significant evidence, let alone particulars. 78 In Balm at para 63, Côté JA stated that an amendment adding an allegation of fraud “likely requires evidence which will pass a stiffer test than that set out in Part C of the body of these reasons.”. See also Condominium Corporation No. 0321365 v. 970365 Alberta Ltd, 2011 ABQB 325, 518 AR 1; Gendreau v. Paramount Structures, 2022 ABQB 34, 2022 CarswellAlta 90, Justice Feth gave the following summary of the law: Principles guiding amendments to pleadings [19] Before or after the close of pleadings, the Court may give permission to amend a pleading: Rule 3.65. [20] The “classic rule” is that amendments are allowed, no matter how careless or late, unless there is prejudice to the other side and the prejudice cannot be repaired (by costs, consequent amendments, an adjournment or other measures): Balm v 3512061 Canada Ltd, 2003 ABCA 98 at para 43 [Balm]; CHS v Alberta (Director of Child Welfare), 2006 ABQB 528at para 11 [CHS]. [21] The classic rule is a “presumption in favor of allowing amendments”: AARC Society v Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, 2019 ABCA 125 at paras 54, 115. The Court's discretion is to be exercised generously: Andritz Ltd v Quality Fabricating and Supply Ltd, 2010 ABQB 101 at para 43. [22] Amendments are therefore generally permitted, subject to “narrow exceptions”: Farm Credit Canada v Chan, 2021 ABCA 168 at para 17 [Farm Credit]. The four established exceptions were confirmed in Domenic Construction Ltd v Primewest Capital Corp, 2020 ABCA 265 at para 20: a. unless permitted by statute, the amendment seeks to add a new party or a new cause of action after the expiry of a limitation period; b. the amendment requested is impermissible, sometimes described as “hopeless” (an amendment that, if it had been in the original pleadings, would have been struck); c. the amendment would cause serious prejudice to the opposing party, not compensable in costs; or d. there is an element of bad faith associated with the failure to plead the amendment in the first instance. See also: Dow Chemical Canada Inc v Nova Chemicals Corporation, 2010 ABQB 524 at paras 20-21. [23] The amount of evidence required to justify an amendment is low; the applicant need not demonstrate that the amended pleading can be proven at trial: Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co Inc v AMEC Americas Limited, 2014 ABCA 74 at paras 24, 26 [Attila]. [24] A “low” or “modest” degree of evidence may justify an amendment to pleadings, even if contradictory evidence is presented: Attila at para 26; Balm at para 29. However, an allegation of fraud “requires evidence which will pass a stiffer test …”: Balm at para 63; and see Balaz v James A Lewis Engineering, 1983 ABCA 90 at para 21; Mikisew Cree First Nation v Canada, 2002 ABCA 110 at para 61. [25] A failure to provide enough evidence to meet the low evidentiary threshold supporting an amendment is sometimes characterized as a “hopeless” amendment: see comments in Attila at para 27. However, the analysis is better understood as a failure to meet the evidentiary threshold for an amendment rather than engaging one of the exceptions. a)—Hopeless amendments [26] The exception for an impermissible or hopeless amendment involves a proposed pleading that, if in the original pleadings, would have been struck for suffering from one or more deficiencies identified in subrules 3.68(2) and (3), which are summarized as follows: a. The Court has no jurisdiction to hear the matter; b. On the face of the proposed pleading, without resorting to evidence, the proposed pleading discloses no reasonable claim or defence to a claim; c. The proposed pleading is frivolous, irrelevant or improper; d. The proposed pleading constitutes an abuse of process; and e. An irregularity in the proposed pleading is so prejudicial to the claim that it is sufficient to defeat the claim. [27] In the normal course, the exception does not otherwise contemplate an inquiry into the merits of the allegation since a summary determination of the facts or questions of mixed fact and law is premature. The pleadings define the scope of discovery and a summary adjudication of the merits usually occurs after each party has a reasonable opportunity to conduct discovery of records and witnesses. Adjudicating the merits of a claim or defence without an adequate evidentiary foundation risks an unjust outcome. [28] Some cases suggest that an amendment will be refused as hopeless where “it is clear that there is no genuine issue for trial, and the amended claim would not survive a summary judgment application”: CHS at para 11. However, these authorities do not invite an adjudication of the merits before discovery nor treat the amendment application as a summary judgment (or dismissal) application. The absence of an arguable claim or defence must be obvious. The inability to resist summary judgment must be plain. The possibility that discovery might alter the assessment of the merits should be considered. [29] Even where discovery is already complete and the amendment will not re-open the discovery process, the logical sequencing is that the pleadings should be clarified before a summary adjudication occurs. In this way, the claims and defences are clearly defined before the Court undertakes the modern approach to summary judgment in which consideration is given to whether the issues and interests involved lend themselves to a “proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result”: Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7 at para 4 [Hryniak]. [30] In Farm Credit, at para 17, the Alberta Court of Appeal confirmed that assessing the likely success of defences, determining whether a defence meets the civil burden of proof, and measuring amendments against the threshold for summary judgment is “usually inappropriate”. Requiring more than a low measure of evidence risks converting an amendment application into a summary judgment application, which is contrary to all principle: Balm at para 29. The pleadings should be settled before dealing with summary judgment: Elbow River Marketing v Canada Clean Fuels Inc, 2011 ABCA 258 at para 4. In short, an amendment application is not a summary adjudication. b)—Bad faith amendments [31] The bad faith exception has received limited judicial interpretation. However, the onus is on the party alleging bad faith to prove it on a balance of probabilities, not on the opposite party to disprove it: Hur v 726913 Alberta Ltd, 2013 ABQB 208 at paras 72, 76 [Hur]. [32] In the absence of something more, amending to defeat a summary judgment application does not demonstrate bad faith: Hur at para 73. [33] In Hur, Justice Russell Brown (as he then was), at para 70, observed that “bad faith” has different meanings depending on the context, although the authorities provide little specific guidance about bad faith as the basis for refusing permission to amend pleadings. He nevertheless found some assistance in comments from CS v MS, 2007 CanLII 20279, 38 RFL (6th) 315 (Ont SCJ) at para 17, affirmed 2010 ONCA 196 [CS], which considered whether a party had engaged in “bad faith” under the costs provisions contained in Ontario's Family Law Rules, O Reg 114/99: In order to come within the meaning of bad faith in subrule 24(8), behaviour must be shown to be carried out with intent to inflict financial or emotional harm on the other party or other persons affected by the behaviour, to conceal information relevant to the issues or to deceive the other party or the court. A misguided but genuine intent to achieve the ostensible goal of the activity, without proof of intent to inflict harm, to conceal relevant information or to deceive, saves the activity from being found to be in bad faith. The requisite intent to harm, conceal or deceive does not have to be the person's sole or primary intent, but rather only a significant part of the person's intent. At some point, a party could be found to be acting in bad faith when their litigation conduct has run the costs up so high that they must be taken to know their behaviour is causing the other party major financial harm without justification. [34] In W. Stevenson and J. Côté, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2021, at 3-127, the editors state that when amending pleadings, bad faith seems to mean an intent to harm, to conceal or to deceive. That interpretation effectively treats bad faith as a specific form of abuse of process arising after the original pleadings were filed. Conversely, an abuse of process caused by the original pleadings is addressed by subrule 3.68(2)(d) and screened as a “hopeless” amendment. [35] Based on the limited authorities, I conclude that the bad faith exception applies to proposed amendments that seek: a. to inflict financial or emotional harm on the adverse party or another person affected by the behaviour; b. to conceal information relevant and material to the litigation issues; or c. to deceive the adverse party or the Court. [36] The exception is not to be used to punish negligent or careless delay that can be remedied through costs. Moreover, the bad faith purpose need not be the applicant's sole or primary intent, so long as a significant feature of the intent was for an abuse of process to occur: CS at para 17. [37] While past litigation conduct may be reviewed to deduce any improper purpose in seeking amendments, the inquiry should be conducted with specificity about how the prior conduct reveals an improper purpose in seeking the particular amendments. A vague and sweeping approach to defining “bad faith” invites an overly expansive, complicated, and expensive application process that can obscure rather than reveal the motivations for specific amendments. The exercise should not digress into sanctioning prior misconduct by denying amendments. [38] Accordingly, an allegation of bad faith does not convert the pleading amendment process into a broad inquiry about the parties' past litigation conduct and the merits of proposed claims and defences, except where the exercise is truly necessary and compelling in showing that specific proposed amendments are motivated by an improper purpose. Otherwise, even modest efforts to clarify issues for discovery and trial convert an interlocutory hearing into a complex and time-consuming exercise. [39] The modern approach to litigation and the operation of the Rules favour timely and cost-effective procedures proportional to the remedy sought: Rule 1.2. The Supreme Court of Canada in Hryniak recognized proportionality as a “touchstone for access to civil justice” and pressed for a culture shift by which judges are to “actively manage the legal process in line with the principle of proportionality”: paras 30 and 32. The risk with an expanded inquiry is that bad faith will be alleged after any long delay and require a lengthy evidentiary record for a robust presentation of the merits. An interlocutory application intended to clarify the issues instead swells and then swamps the proceedings. … [41] The amending process also should not be a preview or substitute for summary adjudication. If the amendment has little or no merit, the opposing party can subsequently seek summary judgment with the advantage of a proper evidentiary record. If the amendment was unnecessary, the additional expense can be addressed through costs, including enhanced costs. [42] The doctrine of abuse of process is flexible and exists to ensure that the administration of justice is not brought into disrepute: Behn v Moulton Contracting Ltd, 2013 SCC 26 at para 41. However, an allegation of bad faith in pursuing an amendment should rarely open the door to an elaborate review of the merits. In Astolfi v. Stone Creek Resorts Inc., 2023 ABKB 416, Justice Marion discussed when an amendment would not be allowed. His Lordship said: [40] The most recent Alberta Court of Appeal framework provides that there is a strong presumption in favour of allowing amendments to pleadings after the close of pleadings: Kosteckyj v Paramount Resources Ltd, 2022 ABCA 230 at paras 12, 41; Pace v Economical Mutual Insurance, 2021 ABCA 1 at para 3; AARC Society v Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, 2019 ABCA 125 at para 85. The applicant need not show any particular reason for needing the amendment: Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co Inc v AMEC Americas Limited, 2014 ABCA 74 at para 24. Courts should exercise their discretion to allow the amendment unless the non-moving party demonstrates an exception or compelling reason not to: Kosteckyj at paras 12, 41; Pace at para 3, 53; AARC Society at paras 6, 53. [41] Courts must consider two distinct interests when assessing the merits of an amendment application: (1) the impact the proposed amendment will have on the non-moving party's litigation interests; and (2) the public interest in the resolution of litigation as quickly as reasonably possible without the expenditure of more public and private resources than is reasonably necessary: AARC Society at paras 57–62. [42] What contemplates a compelling reason not to permit an amendment after the close of pleadings is not, and never has been, a closed list of exceptions. However, while described in different ways by different courts, certain compelling reasons or grounds not to permit amendments have been recognized over time, including: (a) the proposed amendment will significantly harm a legitimate litigation interest of the non-moving party; for example the proposed amendment will cause significant prejudice to a legitimate litigation interest of the non-moving party that cannot adequately be abridged by an ameliorative costs order or any other order: Pace at paras 4–5; Kosteckyj at para 41; AARC Society at para 64; Attila Dogan at para 25; Remington Development Corporation v Enmax Power Corporation, 2022 ABCA 71 at para 33; (b) the proposed amendment advances a claim that cannot possibly succeed or is hopeless because it would have been struck if it were in the original pleading; the test is whether it is plain and obvious that there is no triable issue: Swaleh v Lloyd, 2020 ABCA 18 at para 13; Remington at paras 35–37; Eon Energy Ltd v Ferrybank Resources Ltd, 2018 ABCA 243 at para 18. This incorporates considerations like those under rule 3.68. For example, proposed amendments will be hopeless if they: (i) disclose no cause of action or reasonable claim, or no reasonable defence to a claim: Pace at para 6; AARC Society at para 10; Attila Dogan at para 27; rule 3.68(2)(b); (ii) raise matters over which the court has no jurisdiction: rule 3.68(2)(a); (iii) are frivolous, irrelevant or improper: rule 3.68(2)(c); (iv) constitute an abuse of process: rule 3.68(2)(d); and (v) have an irregularity that is so prejudicial to the claim that it is sufficient to defeat the claim; rule 3.68(2)(e); (c) the proposed amendment is not supported by a required threshold level of evidence, based on the nature of the proposed amendment: Balm v 3512061 Canada Ltd, 2003 ABCA 98 at paras 25–29; Attila Dogan at para 24; Barker v Budget Rent-A-Car of Edmonton Ltd, 2012 ABCA 76 at para 12; Brewin v Magyar, 2022 ABKB 729 at paras 32–33; Club Industrial Trailers v Paramount Structures, 2022 ABQB 34 at para 25; (d) unless permitted by statute, the proposed amendment seeks to add a new party or a new cause of action after the expiry of a limitation period and is statute-barred or subject to a “rock-solid” limitations defence: Attila Dogan at para 25; Pace at para 6; AARC Society at para 65; (e) if the failure to plead earlier, or the proposed amendment itself, involves bad faith: Pace at paras 7, 54; AARC Society at paras 11, 66; Attila Dogan at para 25; and (f) the proposed amendment will contravene the public interest in promoting expeditious and economical dispute resolution: Pace at paras 4, 7, 51–52; Kosteckyj at para 41; AARC Society at paras 59–62. …. [45] A cause of action is a set of facts that provides the basis for an action: Sherwood Steel Ltd v Odyssey Construction Inc, 2014 ABCA 320 at paras 23–24; Markevich v Canada, 2003 SCC 9 at para 27; Bard v Canadian Natural Resources, 2016 ABQB 267 at para 36. [46] In some cases, where an amendment includes a new cause of action not included in the original pleading, an issue may arise as to whether the amendment adequately pleads a cause of action or claim. If it is plain and obvious that it does not, then the amendment is hopeless and will not be allowed: Remington at paras 35–37; Swaleh at para 13. However, courts must allow the amendment, even though it raises a doubtful plea, if it is arguable: Balm at para 12; Oregon Jack Creek Indian Band v Canadian National Railway Co, 1990 CanLII 155 (SCC), [1990] 1 SCR 117 at 118. The test is similar to striking out existing pleadings—a claim will only be struck if it is plain and obvious, assuming the facts pleaded to be true, that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action—one that has no reasonable prospect of success: Balm at para 12; R v Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd, 2011 SCC 42 at paras 17–22; rule 3.68(2)(b); Rudichuk v Genesis Land Development Corp, 2020 ABCA 42 at para 5; RPC Limited Partnership v SNC-Lavalin ATP Inc, 2018 ABCA 423 at para 15. [47] However, where the amendment does not, in substance, raise a new cause of action or claim, but rather provides further factual particulars, seeks additional remedies, or pleads new legal conclusions, relating to or arising out of a cause of action or claim that is already in the original pleading, the amendment alone does not need to have all the elements of a separate or new cause of action or claim: Breen v Foremost Industries Ltd, 2022 ABQB 478 at para 54; Korte v Deloitte, Haskins & Sells, 1996 ABCA 15 at para 27; Bard at paras 36–37; Balm at para 11; Tiger Calcium Services Inc v Sazwan, 2019 ABQB 885 at para 38. Where the original pleading already contained the substance of the allegation, courts may allow amendments that elaborate or provide further particulars on existing claims: Bard at para 37. Particulars are, by definition, further details about the claim originally pleaded: Geophysical Service Incorporated v Plains Midstream Canada ULC, 2021 ABCA 55 at para 5. In these circumstances, the ground to challenge an amendment based on a failure to disclose a cause of action is not necessarily engaged. [48] The court's task is not to look at the amendments in isolation to see if they alone, divorced from the pleading from which they are to be added, disclose a cause of action or reasonable claim. If that was the test, many amendments would fail. The amendments must be considered in the context of the pleading to which they are proposed to be added. [49] Further, like pleadings generally, proposed amendments must be interpreted liberally and generously, not restrictively: Anderson v Airsprint Inc, 2005 ABCA 332 at para 9; PricewaterhouseCoopers Inc v Perpetual Energy Inc, 2021 ABCA 16 at para 74; Tottrup v Lund, 2000 ABCA 121 at para 9; Armstrong v Gula, 2023 ABKB 270 at para 20. …. [60] An amendment that is not supported by sufficient evidence to meet the evidentiary threshold can be considered hopeless: Attila Dogan at para 27; Kichton Contracting Ltd v Giselbrecht, 2022 ABQB 476 at para 15; Ingram v Alberta (Chief Medical Officer of Health), 2022 ABQB 164 at para 35; Brewin at para 32. [61] The evidence threshold for amending pleadings after the close of pleadings depends on the nature or classification of the proposed amendment: Balm at para 25; Hartum (Estate of) v Loewen, 2007 ABCA 15 at para 12; Tiger Calcium at para 38. For example: (a) many amendments require no or minimal evidence. This incudes amendments that are trivial, inconsequential, ancillary or merely clarifying wording: Waquan v Canada, 2002 ABCA 110 at para 26; Balm at para 10; Bard at para 12. It also includes amendments that add new causes of action based on the facts already pleaded: Balm at para 11; Tiger Calcium at para 39; (b) most other significant amendments require only modest evidence and have a low evidentiary threshold: Balm at paras 25, 29; Attila Dogan at paras 24–26; Remington at para 33. The type of “evidence” can be any admissible evidence, but may also include hearsay (see Balm at para 25, citing Marathon Construction (Alberta) Ltd v Bank of Nova Scotia, 1985 CanLII 2517 (SKCA); Green v Redlick, 2023 ABKB 19 at para 10) and possibly even opposing party pleadings: Balm at para 31. But it must have some foundation in fact: Attila at paras 24–26; Bard at para 12; (c) some amendments have a significantly elevated evidentiary threshold. Amendments that add new causes of action based on fraud, high-handedness, or malicious conduct require “significant evidence” establishing a “good ground” or “exceptional circumstances”: Canadian Natural Resources Limited v Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman SA, 2013 ABCA 87 at para 11; Waquan at para 61; Balm at para 63; Tiger Calcium at para 41; Condominium Corporation No. 00311443 v Goertz, 2022 ABQB 104 at para 29; Evanoff Enterprises Ltd v Pioneer Hi-Bred Limited, 2009 ABQB 223 at para 49. A similar elevated evidentiary threshold applies to new allegations of bad faith: Bard at paras 33, 36. However, the elevated threshold does not apply where the amendments add particulars for an existing cause of action: Tiger Calcium at para 42; Bard at para 36. …. [98] A non-moving party may argue that a proposed amendment will cause significant prejudice that cannot adequately be abridged by an ameliorative costs order or any other order: Pace at paras 4–5; Kosteckyj at para 41; AARC Society at para 64; Attila Dogan at para 25; Remington at para 33. [99] The non-moving party has the onus to establish serious prejudice: Bard at para 15. Delay or the passage of time may lead to prejudice: Eon Energy at paras 26–27, citing Matthison v Bradburn (Estate), 2007 ABCA 173; Hunter Financial Group Ltd v Maritime Life Assurance Company, 2009 ABCA 199 at para 9. An inability to defend due to lost witnesses or evidence may lead to prejudice: Bard at para 18; Hunter Financial Group Ltd v Maritime Life Assurance Company, 2007 ABQB 263 at para 12. However, most prejudice will be compensable in costs, including the fact that the amendments may lead to further pleadings and discovery, may lengthen the lawsuit, or are made late in the litigation process: Bard at para 18; Sauvageau v Alberta (Justice and Solicitor General), 2017 ABQB 448 at para 22; Dow Chemical Canada Inc v Nova Chemicals Corporation, 2010 ABQB 524 at para 28; AARC Society at para 93; Kosteckyj at paras 39–42. In Colenutt v. Colenutt, 2023 ABKB 562, Justice Yungwirth referred with approval to Justice Marion's summary (see: paragraphs 22-24; 28; 37-38; 45 of Colenutt). 5. What is a “Cause of Action”? In Sherwood Steel Ltd. v. Odyssey Construction Inc., 2014 ABCA 320, 2014 CarswellAlta 1750, 5 Alta. L.R. (6th) 268, 59 C.P.C. (7th) 221, the Court said, at paragraphs 23–26: [23] What does it mean to re-litigate the same cause of action? The Supreme Court has described a cause of action as “a set of facts that provides the basis for an action”: Markevich v Canada, 2003 SCC 9 (CanLII), 2003 SCC9 at para 27, [2003] 1 SCR 94 [Markevich] (emphasis added). (See also Air Canada v McDonnell Douglas Corp, 1989 CanLII 54 (SCC), [1989] 1 SCR 1554 at 1564, [1989] SCJ No 58 [Air Canada]: “[a] cause of action comprises certain facts which, if proven, establish a plaintiff's right to the remedy sought from the defendant” (emphasis added).) This is consistent with the statement in Black which the chambers judge cited, and with this Court's treatment of “a cause of action” in Madill v Alexander Consulting Group Ltd, 1999 ABCA 321 (CanLII) at para 27, 237 AR 307 [Madill]: “The determination of whether there is a new cause of action requires some assessment of facts, since it is the facts which form the “cause” of the “action”.” (Emphasis added.) [24] A cause of action is, therefore, a set of facts which are said to entitle the claimant to relief from a court. This definition does not, we stress, exclude the possibility that that two distinct causes of action may share some facts. As the Supreme Court said in Grandview at 635-36 (citing this Court's decision in Hall v Hall and Hall's Feed & Grain Ltd (1958), 15 DLR (2d) 638, [1958] AJ No 60 (Alta SCAD): It was apparently the wider principle of res judicata that was applied in the present case. This doctrine has not so wide an application as the broadness of the language might lead one to infer. It is limited to such matters as arise within one cause of action. It is, I think, clear that if there are facts which are common to several causes of action, an inquiry into these facts in one cause of action does not prevent an examination of the same facts where another cause of action is set up, provided that this cause of action is separate and distinct. (Emphasis added.) [25] Nor does this definition of cause of action preclude two separate causes of action arising from the same subject matter. In other words, a cause of action is not the same as another merely because they share subject matter. In Chand and Chand v Sabo Bros Realty Ltd et al (1977), 1977 CanLII 678 (AB QB), 10 AR 352 at para 24, 81 DLR (3d) 382 (QB), aff'd (with variation of quantum) (1979), 1979 ALTASCAD 5 (CanLII), 14 AR 302, [1979] 2 WWR 248 [Chand], the same failed real estate transaction formed the subject matter for both a cause of action against the realtors (alleging breach of a duty of care) and a cause of action against the owner/seller “(alleging breach of the contract of sale).” Similarly, in Glenko, the same breach of trust by the appellant's company was the subject not only of an action against the company for breach of trust, but also against the appellant for a declaration that certain properties held by him were subject to a constructive trust. [26] Further, the fact that two actions request identical relief does not necessarily mean that they each assert the same cause of action. In Petersen Pontiac Buick GMC (Alta) Ltd v Campbell, 2013 ABCA 251 (CanLII) [Peterson Pontiac Buick] at paras 18, 28–30, 556 AR 118, this Court held that the trial judge properly identified separate and distinct causes of action despite each of them supporting claims for identical damages. This is significant here, as Sherwood seeks the same relief ($216,792.27) in its action against Odyssey as it sought in its action against Edmonton Concrete. And, both actions share the same subject matter: Edmonton Concrete's unpaid debt for rebar. These similarities, on their own, do not demonstrate that identical causes of action were asserted in both actions. What matters, as Air Canada, Grandview, Madill and Markevich make clear, are the facts that are said to give rise to an entitlement to relief. And here, the facts which Sherwood Steel relies upon to support its claim against Odyssey are different from those upon which it relied in obtaining judgment against Edmonton Concrete. In Agreecomm Construction Inc. Westvillage Condominiums Ltd., 2013 ABPC 327, 2013 CarswellAlta 2467, plaintiffs applied to amend their civil claims. The question was whether the proposed amendments added a new cause of action outside the statutory limitation period. New Action Added after Limitation Period Expires There are two approaches to the question of whether an amendment ought to be permitted after the expiration of a limitation date: the functional approach which requires the party opposing the amendment to show that the amendment will cause actual prejudice, and the analytical approach which requires the party seeking the amendment to show special circumstances. In a nutshell, if one's action is governed by the old Limitations of Actions Act, then the analytical approach applies [see: Madill v. Alexander Consulting Group Ltd. (1999), 237 A.R. 307 (C.A.)]. If one's action is governed by the new Limitations Act, then the functional approach applies [see: Stout Estate v. Golinowski Estate (2002), 299 A.R. 13 (C.A.)]. In Madill v. Alexander Consulting Group Ltd. (1999), 237 A.R. 307 (C.A.), Madam Justice Russell said, at pp. 321-24: The leading authority on the amendment of pleadings after the expiry of a limitation period is the Supreme Court of Canada decision in Basarsky v. Quinlan[(1972), 24 D.L.R. (3d) 720]. Onishenko died in a motor vehicle accident. His administrator, Basarsky, commenced an action against the Quinlans pursuant to provisions under the Trustee Act. After the expiry of the relevant limitation periods, Basarsky sought to amend the statement of claim to add a claim on behalf of Onishenko's widow and children pursuant to the Fatal Accidents Act. As can be deduced from the reasons, the application for the amendment was made after examinations for discovery had been conducted during which questions were asked regarding the widow's employment, and the number and ages of the children. The reasons delivered by Hall, J., were relatively brief. He discussed the rule in Weldon v. Neal (1887), 56 L.J.Q.B. 621 (C.A.), which was a case where an amendment sought to add a new cause of action, and focussed on the fact that the rule in Weldon v. Neal provided for exceptions where there are “peculiar circumstances”. In his view, the term “peculiar” can be equated with “special” in current usage. And he found those circumstances in Basarsky because all the facts relating to the tort and the respondents [sic] liability were pleaded in the original statement of claim, the respondents admitted liability, and the examination for discovery included questions relevant only to a Fatal Accidents Act action. He further held that the respondents were not “actually” prejudiced by the failure to name the Fatal Accidents Act in the original statement of claim, since in Alberta, unlike some other jurisdictions, failure to give particulars was not a reason to strike the statement of claim as disclosing no cause of action. The reasons of Hall, J., show that the rule in Weldon v. Neal still applied subject to exceptions where peculiar or special circumstances exist. Hall, J.'s, reasons suggest that the absence of actual prejudice is a factor which may contribute to the establishment of special circumstances but is not the single most significant criteria. By emphasising special circumstances and considering actual prejudice, Basarsky modifies the rule in Weldon v. Neal rendering it less likely that a mere technicality will defeat litigation. However, in Basarsky, Hall, J., did not employ the functional approach. Rather, the functional approach was first proposed by Professor Watson in his article, “Amendment of Proceedings After Expiry of Limitation Period”, [(1975), 53 Can. Bar Rev. 237], and is clearly a different test than the analytical approach as embodied in Weldon v. Neal and expanded in Basarsky. The presumptions and onus of proof in the two approaches are contra-posed. The functional approach is characterised by the central question of whether the amendment will in fact prejudice the defendant in his/her defence of the action at trial. It presumes the amendment should be granted unless the party opposing can show actual prejudice. In contrast, the analytical approach presumes the amendment should not be granted unless the party seeking the amendment can show special circumstances. The Chambers judge in this case recognized that there are two theoretical lines of reasoning which have developed in Alberta regarding amendments to a statement of claim after the expiration of a limitation period. But after reviewing the decision of Lefsrud, J., in Bank of Nova Scotia v. Lennie et al. (1995), 167 A.R. 45 (Q.B.), she went on to conclude that “the question of which approach to adopt may be a technical one, with the real question being whether or not it is in the interests of justice to allow such an amendment”… She found support for this proposition in the reasons of this court in Davidson Partners Ltd. et al. v. Del Rio International et al. (1995), 174 A.R. 386 (C.A.), and Korte et al. v. Cormie et al.[(1996), 178 A.R. 199 (C.A.)]… She held that in the reasons of Hunt, J.A., in Korte, the functional and analytical approaches were amalgamated to form a test in which “[t]he question of the interests of justice is answered by a consideration of any special circumstances in the case, including any prejudice which would be suffered by the party opposing the amendment.”… That interpretation of those reasons does not correctly state the test for amendments after expiry of limitation periods. First, to suggest the choice between the tests is technical only and that they can be amalgamated, ignores the fact that the two tests have opposite presumptions of whether or not the amendment should be allowed, and on whom the onus lies to defeat the presumption. Second, it fails to consider that this court has never applied the functional approach. In Davidson Partners v. Del Rio International, supra, this court at p. 387 specifically declined to approve or disapprove of the functional approach which was adopted by the Chambers judge. Nor does that case support the view that lack of prejudice is sufficient to establish special circumstances. On appeal, this court noted other factors, in addition to lack of prejudice, which constituted special circumstances. The claim against the corporate defendant included promissory notes signed by the individual defendant. After the expiration of the limitation period, the individual defendant filed a defence denying he signed in his personal capacity. The application under appeal sought to amend the claim to include a personal claim against the individual defendant. This court concluded that the defendant understood the broader impact of the original claim, and hence, the amendment was merely technical. Third, the Chambers judge misinterpreted Hunt, J.A., in Korte v. Cormie, who did not have to decide which test applied because, there, the issue was whether leave to amend was required. The plaintiffs had sought to amend their pleadings which originally had excepted out one of the many defendants from one of the five causes of action. They later sought to delete the exception and in effect, claim a new cause against one of the original named defendants. The new cause was conspiracy to defraud. No statement of defence had been filed, so, the primary issue was whether leave was required to amend the statement of claim. One of the alternative arguments was that if the limitation period had expired, leave should be required. Whether the limitation period had expired was unclear. Hunt, J.A., in giving the decision of the court, reviewed cases granting amendment after the limitation period had expired, but did not adopt either the functional or analytical approach. She held that if there is a possible limitations defence, leave to amend should be required. She upheld the order of the Chambers judge which permitted the amendment but preserved the defendant's right to raise the limitations defence. She stated at p. 208, in a situation where the amendment raises the possibility of a limitation argument: The judge hearing such an application for leave to amend has a number of choices. He or she may agree that the new claim is out of time and thus disallow the amendment; may determine that the sort of special circumstances referred to in Basarsky exist, and allow the amendment nevertheless; or decide that the limitation argument is of the kind that ought to be determined at trial, upon a factual base. In that statement, Hunt, J.A., was simply describing the options of the strict application of the rule in Weldon v. Neal, or the adoption of the special circumstances exception as set out in Basarsky. In either case, the test is the analytical approach and not the functional approach. In referring to Basarsky, Hunt, J.A., should not be interpreted to advocate an amalgamation of the two approaches because that case did not do so, nor did it apply the functional test to determine whether to permit an amendment after expiry of a limitation. Other provinces appear to take a functional approach to amendments after the expiry of limitations periods. In those cases, however, there is a statutory basis for departing from the test as set out in Basarsky. . . . . . No similar statutory provision has been adopted in Alberta. Consequently, in this province, the test in Basarsky must be applied. Thus, the respondents in this appeal must show that special circumstances exist to permit an exception to the general rule that amendments after expiry of limitation periods are not allowed. There is no onus upon the appellants to show prejudice, although, the absence of any evidence of prejudice to the appellants would assist the respondents in establishing their argument. As the reasons of Hall, J., suggest, absence of actual prejudice is one factor contributing to the establishment of special circumstances. The initial inquiry, however, is not whether there would be prejudice. It remains to be considered whether the Chambers judge erred in deferring to the trial judge the determination of whether there are the sort of special circumstances contemplated by the exception in Basarky. Did the Chambers judge err in deferring to the trial judge the question of whether there are any special circumstances outweighing prejudice to the appellants? In my view, Basarsky, supra, requires the respondent to show some special circumstances, in addition to lack of prejudice to the appellants. Here, the only special circumstances that the respondents could point to was the expert's 1997 report showing the extent of damage suffered as a result of the inability to commutate the pension funds prior to the end of 1988, and concluding that the appellants were negligent in failing to warn the respondent in that regard. All of the material evidence necessary to determine whether that report established special circumstances was before the Chambers judge. And since no other special circumstances were alleged, there was no rationale for deferring this issue to the trial judge. The retention of an expert who provided further and better legal advice does not constitute special circumstances. The lack of appreciation of the full extent of legal or financial consequences of material facts is not relevant to the establishment of a cause of action. And in any event, the special circumstances which were alleged were not sufficient, in my view, to overcome the prejudice to the appellants.
