She made no palpable and overriding error in concluding that non-compensable prejudice would arise if FastTrack were allowed to amend its counterclaim to add claims for specific performance of the purchase contract for the lands, and to add the proposed new parties. In Provalcid Inc. v. Graff, 2015 ABQB 574, Justice Yamauchi made the following comment about prejudice: 23 As for the lateness or delay in a party seeking to amend its pleadings, Graesser J said the following in John Barlot Architect Ltd v 973189 Alberta Ltd, 2008 ABQB 458 at para 22: • From a review of the case law, the following principles emerge: a) amendments will be presumptively allowed, no matter how late, provided there is no prejudice that cannot be adequately compensated in costs; b) the onus is on the person opposing the amendment to show that the amendment will result in prejudice that cannot be adequately compensated; c) it is trite law that an amendment will be permitted where it can be made without prejudice; d) mere delay or procrastination in amending pleadings are not sufficient reasons in themselves to deny the amendment; and e) generally, amendments ought to be allowed in order to assure a full resolution of the controversies between the parties. 24 Despite these comments, other courts have held that delay itself might be prejudicial. See e.g. Hunter Financial Group Ltd v Maritime Life Assurance Co, 2007 ABQB 263, 428 AR 150, 75 Alta LR (4th) 165 [Hunter, cited to ABQB]. In a different context, in 375850 Alberta Ltd v Noel, 2012 ABCA 372, 78 Alta LR (5th) 39 [Noel, cited to ABCA] at paras 24-25, the Alberta Court of Appeal commented on statutorily-enacted limitation periods when it said: • First, when there is a one-year time limit for filing a complaint, one cannot allow any and every amendment to a complaint after the year has passed. One could not (for example) tack a totally different complaint onto an old filed complaint. That would make a mockery of the time limit. Here the complaint as filed and presented to the Tribunal was clearly discrimination in employment, and nothing else. Now, on a second level of appeal, it is proposed to substitute discrimination in public accommodation. Public accommodation is a brand-new topic, and a brand-new ground to complain. That substantially evades the one-year limit. • And the Legislature does not give time limits for complaints or lawsuits just out of a sense of tidiness. […] A belated complaint can be very unfair, and difficult to remember, investigate, or to defend oneself against. Raising a complaint after the time set by the Legislature leads to a natural inference that there is some prejudice to the person accused. Here the appellant's factum was filed over six years after the events in question, and so over five years after the time limit expired. The inference of prejudice is thus strong. The Alberta Human Rights Act does not look only at the interests of those complaining of discrimination. It also gives some rights to those accused. 25 In Dow Chemical, Wittmann CJQB discussed the situation where limitation periods might have expired. He said the following: • Traditionally, when there is an issue of limitations and an amendment is sought, a court may: 1. Determine the limitation period has not expired and allow the amendment. 2. Rule the limitation period has expired and therefore consider s. 6 of the Limitations Act which provides for when an amendment can be made beyond the limitation period. 3. Find that because of uncertainty in the evidence, the amendments should be allowed subject to the determination of the limitation issue at trial: Hill v. Hill, [2007] A.J. No. 1515 (Alta. Q.B. [In Chambers]) at para. 22, aff'd 2007 ABCA 293 (Alta. C.A.) at para. 10. • A variation of the last option is to determine whether s. 6(2)(b) of the Limitations Act saves a claim otherwise barred by the statute. • Dow Chemical at para 64. In Ponto v. Wawanesa Mutual Insurance Company, 2024 ABKB 669, Justice Harris said that there is no presumption of prejudice when amendments are sought at a late stage of the litigation. Justice Harris said: [53] The concept of a presumption of prejudice when amendments are sought at a late stage in the litigation is raised in Eon Energy Ltd v Ferrybank Resources Ltd, 2018 ABCA 243. There, the defendant sought to amend its pleadings on the eve of trial, but its application was denied by the trial judge, partly on the basis that the proposed amendments would cause serious prejudice not compensable in costs. The proposed amendments “fundamentally” changed the issues at trial after four years of litigation, extending the focus to events which occurred more than 13 years earlier and completely contradicting the position the defendant had taken throughout the litigation. The trial judge found that the amendments meant the trial could not proceed as scheduled, and that the defendant could have sought the amendment much earlier in time. In reliance upon 422252 Alberta Ltd. v Messenger, 2013 ABQB 399, the trial judge stated: Even if the limitation period as submitted by Ferrybank has not passed with respect to its request for a declaration that Eon has no interest in the wells, and on the basis that there is a continuing action constantly re-setting the limitation as Ferrybank has submitted, the matters relevant to the determination of title occurred more than ten years ago. There is, therefore, a presumption of prejudice given the long passage of time and I find that Ferrybank has not rebutted this presumption. (emphasis added) [54] In upholding the trial decision, the Court of Appeal provides no clear comment on whether the trial judge's statement regarding the existence of a presumption of prejudice was correct or not. Rather, other decisions were reviewed as supportive of the trial judge's decision. For example, in Hartum (Estate of) v Loewen, 2007 ABCA 15, amendments were refused when a three-week trial had already been set, experts reports were nearly ready, seven rounds of questioning had taken place and the tremendous amount of work that had taken place all caused real prejudice to the respondent. In Matthison v Bradburn (Estate), 2007 ABCA 173, amendments were refused on the morning of trial in a case which had been commenced ten years earlier and the need for amendments had been apparent many years before. [55] Eon is cited regularly in subsequent decisions from this Court dealing with amendments to pleadings, but there is little to no comment upon whether a presumption of prejudice applies if amendments are sought after a certain time frame. In Brewin v Magyar, 2022 ABKB 729, the Court notes at para 28, that: It will be easier to establish serious prejudice not compensable in costs where the amendments relate to events that occurred long ago, there have been many years of litigation on original pleadings, new amendments fundamentally change the issues, and the amendments will cause further delay such as adjournment of a trial or the need to redo questioning and production of records: Eon Energy, paras 19-28; Jin v Ren, 2014 ABQB 250, paras 31-32; and Precision Forest Industries Ltd v East Prairie Investments Corp, 2018 ABQB 489 (M.), paras 48-49. [56] In Jin, the Court found that amendments were sought at a very late stage in the proceedings, attempted to introduce new representations and allegations, withdrew admissions, and raised defences without having met the prerequisites. In Precision Forest Industries, the Court cites Messenger and concludes that the respondent had met its burden of showing it would suffer non compensable prejudice were the amendments to be allowed when it had been over 14 years since the agreement which formed the basis of the litigation had been signed. The Court notes at para 48 that, “this is a significant period of time and its passage is detrimental to the availability and that quality of evidence”. [57] In Woodbridge Homes Inc v Andrews, 2019 ABQB 585, the Court commented at para 21 that, Amendments proposed even at a very late stage of a civil proceeding are permitted under the general rule, provided that the amendments do not prejudice the opposite party or fall into one of the other exceptions. For example, if all the evidence has already been completed without reference to an issue not raised by the pleadings, prejudice will be virtually inevitable: McDonald v Fellows (1979), 1979 ABCA 224 (CanLII), 17 AR 330 at 336 (Alta CA) [58] Most recently, in RK v GSG, 2024 ABKB 661 at para 7 the Court notes that if an opposing party objects to the proposed amendments, that party bears the onus of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the amendment falls within one of the exceptions, citing Foda v Capital Health Legion, 2007 ABCA 207 and AARC Society at para 53. [59] The statement of the trial judge in Eon about a presumption of prejudice is an outlier. There is no such presumption. To conclude otherwise would reverse the burden of proof. Other decisions (including those relying upon Eon) confirm that a respondent still bears the burden of proving prejudice, even after a significant passage of time. However, that burden becomes progressively easier to meet the longer the action has been outstanding, and the more steps have been taken to prepare for trial – to the point where it might become “inevitable”. See also “Is Evidence Necessary?” under this rule. 18. Amending Style of Cause After Expiration of Limitation Period In Fiebich v. Ortlieb, 2004 ABCA 256, 2004 CarswellAlta 1132, 354 A.R. 279, 31 Alta. L.R. (4th) 1, O'Leary J.A., speaking for the Court, discussed the amendment of a style of cause after the expiration of the limitation period, and the issue of whether an action is a nullity. In Fiebich, the father of two deceased minors commenced an action in relation to their July 11, 1990 deaths. In the action, he described himself as “the Administrator of the Estates” of the children. In fact, he was not so appointed, and in 1999, the children's mother obtained an order appointing her as administratrix ad litem of the estates “for the purpose of the within action”. The style of cause was amended accordingly. No objection was taken to that amendment. Subsequently, on May 2, 2000, the mother was granted letters of administration in respect of the children's estates, and in August, 2000, she applied to amend the statement of claim by amending the style of cause again to reflect her position as administratrix, and to add to the action claims for loss of future earnings. The Court of Appeal allowed the amendment of the style of cause, and denied the amendment that would have added the claims for loss of future earnings. The latter ruling is set out in the annotation to this Rule entitled “New Action Added after Limitation Period Expires”. As to the amendment of a style of cause after the expiration of a limitation period, O'Leary J.A. said, at pp. 7-9: In Stout Estate v. Golinowski Estate this court held that an action commenced within the limitation period on behalf of an estate by an administrator ad litem appointed for that purpose by a court order was not a nullity but merely an irregularity. It could be cured by amendment of the style of cause outside the limitation period to substitute the duly appointed administrator of the estate. In Stout Estate, claims were advanced by the administrator ad litem on behalf of the estate and on behalf of the deceased's parents for dependency. The defendant applied to strike the statement of claim as disclosing no cause of action on the ground an administrator ad litem cannot, in law, sue on behalf of an estate. Prior to the application being heard, the administrator ad litem was formally appointed administrator of the estate. The administrator then cross-applied to amend the style of cause accordingly. The Chambers judge granted the application to strike and dismissed the application to amend. He held the action was a nullity ab initio and the style of cause could not be amended after expiry of the limitation period. On appeal, the court distinguished the circumstances from cases where an administrator commences an action on behalf of an estate before formal appointment, or where one of the parties is non-existent (deceased, for example) when the action is commenced, which could give rise to characterization of the action as a nullity. Although the appointment of the administrator ad litem to commence the action was improper since an administrator ad litem has been held to lack capacity to commence actions as a representative, the court recognized that the order appointing the administrator ad litem had not been appealed and remained valid until set aside. It was not void ab initio and the action could not, therefore, be characterized as a nullity. The court in Stout Estate relied on an earlier decision of the court, Frank v. Canada (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Affairs) (1987), 88 A.R. 241, 56 Alta. L.R. (2d) 289 (C.A.), the unanimous decision of a five-member panel. There, the court expressly disagreed with the proposition that an order appointing an administrator ad litem to defend an action on behalf of an estate where an administrator had already been appointed should be characterized as void ab initio and a nullity. The court permitted the substitution of the administrator for the administrator ad litem. The court in Stout Estate held at para. 75 that [t]here was a validly, but irregularly appointed, administrator ad litem and a properly constituted action brought on the authority of that appointment. Even if the appointment [of the administrator ad litem] may be validly set aside, neither it, nor the action brought on the basis of it, is a nullity. The court concluded that the principle in Frank should be extended to situations where an action is commenced on behalf of an estate by a court-appointed administrator ad litem. It was held in Stout Estate that neither the order appointing the administrator ad litem nor the claim brought under its authority were nullities. Naming the administrator ad litem as the representative plaintiff was an irregularity. The critical question was whether the irregularity could and should be cured by amendment to substitute the properly appointed general administrator. The order of December 21, 1999 appointing Debby Fiebich administratrix ad litem was for the express purpose of continuing the action on behalf of the infants' estates. The defendants raised no objection to the order and it was never appealed, varied or set aside. It remains valid despite the fact it should not have been made. The claims of the estates were validated by the order. Following the appointment of Debby Fiebich as administratrix ad litem, the status of the claims made on behalf of the estates was as if they had been commenced by her in that capacity within the limitation period. Neither the appointment nor the claims of the estates could be characterized as nullities. For the reasons expressed by this court in Stout Estate and Frank v. King Estate, I conclude that the claims brought on behalf of the infants' estates were not nullities but, rather, curable irregularities. The issue is whether the irregularities can and should be cured by substituting Debby Fiebich in her capacity as administrator after expiry of the limitation period. 19. Misnomer … the proper test to be applied in cases of determining whether or not there has been a misnomer is to ask the question—would a reasonable person reading the document understand that he is the person referred to therein but wrongly named or named under a pseudonym? If so, it is a matter of misnomer and the court will permit amendment of the pleadings in order to properly identify the party. If such is not the case, the rule is that it is not a case of misnomer but simply an attempt to introduce a new party by way of addition or substitution. Brochner v. MacDonald (1988), 56 Alta. L.R. (2d) 72 at 76 (Q.B.). The Court of Appeal has said the same thing: Where an original defendant knows whom the plaintiff intends to sue and that from the statement of claim it is not the one the plaintiff intends to sue and it is clear who the proper defendant is, which is the situation in this instance, then it is a case of misnomer and the amendment should be allowed. J.R. Sheet Metal & Manufacturing Ltd. v. Prairie Wood Products (1980) Ltd. (1986), 42 Alta. L.R. (2d) 378 (C.A.), at 381, per McDermid J.A. In J.R. Sheet Metal & Manufacturing Ltd. v. Prairie Wood Products (1980) Ltd. (1986), 42 Alta. L.R. (2d) 378 (C.A.), Stevenson J.A., as he then was, agreed with the majority's conclusion and, at p. 382, said “the Supreme Court of Canada has approved the application of the test in Davies v. Elsby Bros. Ltd.”. Though his Lordship expressed concerns about the Davies test, he agreed that it correctly set forth the current state of the law on misnomer. The test set forth by Lord Justice Devlin in Davies v. Elsby Brothers Ltd., [1960] 3 All E.R. 672 (C.A.), is set out as follows at p. 676: The test must be: How would a reasonable person receiving the document take it? If, in all the circumstances of the case and looking at the document as a whole, he would say to himself: “Of course it must mean me, but they have got my name wrong”, then there is a case of mere misnomer. If, on the other hand, he would say: “I cannot tell from the document itself whether they mean me or not and I shall have to make inquiries”, then it seems to me that one is getting beyond the realm of misnomer. One of the factors which must operate on the mind of the recipient of a document, and which operates in this case, is whether there is or is not another entity to whom the description on the writ might refer. In Rocklake Enterprises Ltd. v. Timberjack Inc., 2001 ABCA 191, 2001 CarswellAlta 1045, 293 A.R. 124, 94 Alta. L.R. (3d) 257, Côté J.A., speaking for the majority, said, at p. 268: Besides, those authorities which call for an objective test and ask what the reasonable reader of the statement of claim would realize, emphasize that that must be done without further inquiry. … I am not aware of any authority which lets one change a party after the limitation period expires because the other party could have conducted research which would have revealed the error. In Nichwolodoff v. Edmonds, 2001 ABQB 613, 2001 CarswellAlta 954, 291 A.R. 384, 93 Alta. L.R. (3d) 153 (Q.B.), Lefsrud J. gave the following summary of the law regarding amendments in cases of misnomer. At pp. 157-158, his Lordship said: Amendments may be made to a statement of claim despite the expiration of the applicable limitation period if the misnaming of a party was a mere “misnomer” (Ladouceur v. Howarth (1973), 41 D.L.R. (3d) 416 (S.C.C.)). The proper form of analysis for cases of misnomer was set out in Nagy v. Phillips (1996), 137 D.L.R. (4th) 715 (Alta. C.A.). The following questions must be addressed: 1. Is this a case of misnomer according to the test set out in Davies v. Elsby Brothers Ltd.… 2. If so, were the Defendants misled or substantially injured by the misnomer? 3. Did the Plaintiff show due diligence, or a lack of unreasonable delay, in finding out the correct names of the Defendants and applying to amend to substitute them in the Statement of Claim? This last point was also noted by Moen J. in Bell v. Chana, 2006 ABQB 139, 2006 CarswellAlta 882, 403 A.R. 115, 60 Alta. L.R. (4th) 320, at p. 331: In a misnomer case, the judge should not grant an application to substitute a defendant unless “…the applicant has been reasonably diligent to seek to properly identify the desired defendant.” See also the annotations under “Test of Misnomer” and “Correction of Misnomer” under R. 38. 20. Effective Date of Amendment The amendment relates back to the commencement of the action. See Owens v. Calgary Farmer (The), [1927] 3 W.W.R. 62 (Alta. T.D.). The amendments to the statement of claim are effective and take effect from the date the statement of claim was issued. Bernard v. Yurich (1987), 81 A.R. 1 at 11 (Master). In Korte v. Cormie (1996), 36 Alta. L.R. (3d) 431 (C.A.), Madam Justice Hunt, speaking for the court, said, at p. 443: The authorities suggest that an amendment usually dates from the date of the statement of claim… However, where an amendment is permitted that adds a new cause of action, the Court may order that the new cause of action takes effect only from the date of the amendment. 21. Withdrawing Representation Made By Counsel Regarding Claim In Chenen Resources Ltd. v. EnCana Corp., 2006 ABQB 931, 2006 CarswellAlta 2050, 411 A.R. 1, an action was commenced against EnCana by the plaintiff, Chenen Resources alleging breaches of a gas marketing agreement. Counsel for EnCana asked counsel for Chenen if the plaintiff “was going to pursue a claim for damages relating to the exploration and production aspect” of certain business which occurred in November 2004 (described as the CanEnerco business). Counsel for Chenen replied that “I can now confirm that the damages claimed in this action are not with respect to the Exploration and Production aspect of CanEnerco's business. The primary focus of the damages are the other two aspects: namely, marketing and gas storage business.” Wilkins J. held that the words “the primary focus of the damages are the two other aspects” should be “interpreted as a binding representation that Chenen will conduct their case in a particular manner. So categorized, leave of the Court is required for Chenen to withdraw it.” At p. 8, Wilkins J. said: 48 The test for that leave is in my opinion correctly set forth in Edmonton (City) v. Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc., [2000] A.J. No. 87. In that case, the Court concluded that a representation of counsel was tantamount to an amendment of the plaintiff's proceeding to withdraw a claim. Justice Lee concluded that the test for leave to withdraw in relation to such a representation is the same as for a further amendment of a pleading to reassert that claim. That is, it will be permitted where it can be made without prejudice to the opposite party which cannot be compensated in costs, there is no undue delay; and no limitation defence would be lost to the defendant. 22. Concurrent applications to amend and to strike In Hur v. 726913 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 208, Mr. Justice Brown said: 27 Where an application for summary judgment is heard concurrently with a cross-application for permission to amend pleadings, the Court must determine the amendment application first before determining the application for summary judgment. (Elbow River Marketing Limited Partnership v. Canada Clean Fuels Inc., 2011 ABCA 258 at para. 3) It appears, from the face of Master Breitkreuz's order, that he followed this procedure, deferring consideration of summary judgment until the state of the pleadings had been determined: he first denied the Plaintiffs' application to amend the Statement of Claim, then summarily dismissed the Plaintiffs' claim against the Defendants. An example of the application of this direction is found in Michael Awad Professional Corp. v. 531845 Alberta Inc., 2015 ABQB 296 (Master). Master Robertson said: 14 Before oral arguments got underway, I drew to the attention of the parties Hur v. 726913 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 208 at para. 27, where the Court said that where there are cross-applications both for summary judgment and to amend the claim the court must hear and decide the application to amend before considering summary judgment. Also, in Chevalier v. Sunshine Village Corporation, 2011 ABQB 544, the Master allowed an application to amend to be brought before making his decision on an application to strike under Rule 3.68. 15 Accordingly, although the applications were argued together, it is incumbent upon the Court to decide the amendment application before deciding the application to strike. 16 It is not necessary for the defendant to bring a new application to strike; it is possible to deal with the application to strike taking into account the amended pleading, if in fact an amendment is allowed. The Court must simply look at the proposed amended pleading instead of the original one to determine if it discloses a reasonable cause of action. 17 The application is made a little awkward by the fact that on an application to amend, there must be affidavit evidence filed in support to substantiate the need for the amendments. In contrast, on an application to strike under Rule 3.68, the court is required to look only at the pleading and not at evidence. Accordingly, I must consider the evidence that has been filed in support of the application to amend, but then ignore it for the application to strike.

BOOK_C.title: Permission of Court to amendment before or after close of pleadings
BOOK_C.division_heading: Division 4 – REQUEST FOR PARTICULARS, AMENDMENTS TO PLEADINGS AND CLOSE OF PLEADINGS
BOOK_C.operative_text_raw:
(1) Subject to subrule (5), before or after close of pleadings, the Court may give permission to amend a pleading.
(2) If the Court gives permission for a pleading to be amended, the Court must specify the time period within which the amended pleading must be filed and served.
(3) An order giving permission to amend a pleading under this rule ceases to have effect unless the amended pleading is filed and served within the time specified by the Court.
(4) If the Court directs or allows a pleading to be amended at trial, (a) the amendment must be recorded in writing by the court clerk, and (b) no order need be filed.
(5) This rule does not apply to an amendment to a pleading to add, remove, substitute or correct the name of a party to which rule 3.74 [Adding, removing or substituting parties after close of pleadings] applies.

commentary.text:
Rule 3.65 gives the court jurisdiction and discretion to amend a pleading, but gives no substantive guidelines on when amendments not adding parties should be granted, merely stating that “the Court may give permission to amend a pleading.” Armstrong v. Gula (Litigation Representative of), [2024] A.J. No. 741, 2024 ABKB 358 at paras. 124-127 (Alta. K.B.) provides a good summary of the law outlined below, citing many of the relevant cases.
Unlike former rule 132, it does not indicate the need for the purpose of determining the real question in issue between the parties. However, the effect is the same by virtue of rule 1.2(2)(a), which includes that purpose in the overall purpose and intention of the new Alberta Rules of Court. Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v. Crossroads C & I Distributors, [2011] A.J. No. 91, 2011 ABQB 51 at paras. 42-44 (Alta. Q.B.). For completeness rule 3.65 should be read in conjunction with rule 3.62.160 Court’s Discretion – The power to allow amendments is discretionary. Wood Buffalo Housing & Development Corp. v.
